summary: Traffic-engineering link attributes were first used with RSVP-TE, but newer applications like Segment Routing Policy and Loop-Free Alternates also use them. The existing advertisements can't carry application-specific values or show which applications use them. This document defines IS-IS advertisements that can. It obsoletes RFC 8919.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS routers advertise facts about each link, such as its bandwidth and delay, so that other routers can plan paths. This document adds a way to say which application each fact is meant for, so two different applications can be given different values for the same link.

subtitle: IS-IS extensions that let a link say different traffic engineering values to different applications.

tldr.problem: IS-IS advertises link attributes such as bandwidth and delay, but the advertisements do not say which application is meant by them. In a network running both RSVP-TE and Segment Routing Policy, a router can read a link attribute as a sign that RSVP-TE is enabled on a link where it is not, and the two applications cannot be given different values for the same link.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines two new advertisements, an Application-Specific Link Attributes sub-TLV and an Application-Specific SRLG TLV, and a bit mask that names the applications the attributes belong to. A legacy flag lets the new advertisements point back at the old ones.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9479 replaces RFC 8919 and clarifies when zero-length bit masks must and must not be used. The new advertisements stay optional: a network with routers that do not understand them keeps using the old ones.

today: RFC 9479 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 8919, and it is the current definition of the IS-IS Application-Specific Link Attributes sub-TLV and the Application-Specific SRLG TLV.

sections.title: Why Link Attributes Need Application Names
sections.content:
Advertisement of link attributes by the IS-IS protocol in support of Traffic Engineering was introduced by RFC 5305 and extended by RFC 5307, RFC 6119, RFC 7308 and RFC 8570. The use of these extensions has been associated with deployments supporting traffic engineering over MPLS in the presence of RSVP, more succinctly RSVP-TE.

New applications with use cases for many of the same link attributes have been introduced, including Segment Routing Policy and Loop-Free Alternates. That has introduced ambiguity. If a deployment mixes RSVP-TE support with SR Policy support, it is not possible to say unambiguously which advertisements are for RSVP-TE and which are for SR Policy. If the topologies are fully congruent this may not matter, but any incongruence leads to ambiguity.

An example is a network where RSVP-TE is enabled only on a subset of its links. A link attribute is advertised for another application on a link that is not enabled for RSVP-TE. As soon as the router that is an RSVP-TE head end sees the attribute, it assumes RSVP-TE is enabled on that link, and any RSVP-TE path it tries to set up through that link fails.

A second issue arises where both applications are supported on a link but the values differ per application, because the current advertisements cannot carry application-specific values for the same attribute on the same link.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers advertise facts about their links so that path planning can use them. The facts do not say which program is meant to use them, so when two different programs need different values for the same link, there is no way to express that.

sections.title: The Existing Link Attribute Advertisements
sections.content:
The existing advertisements used in support of RSVP-TE include sub-TLVs for TLVs Advertising Neighbor Information and TLVs for Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) advertisements. The sub-TLV values are defined in the IS-IS Sub-TLVs for TLVs Advertising Neighbor Information registry, and the TLVs in the IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry.

The legacy sub-TLVs are type 3 administrative group (color), 9 maximum link bandwidth, 10 maximum reservable link bandwidth, 11 unreserved bandwidth, 14 extended administrative group, 18 TE default metric, 33 unidirectional link delay, 34 min/max unidirectional link delay, 35 unidirectional delay variation, 36 unidirectional link loss, 37 unidirectional residual bandwidth, 38 unidirectional available bandwidth and 39 unidirectional utilized bandwidth.

The legacy SRLG advertisements are TLV 138, which supports links identified by IPv4 addresses and unnumbered links, and TLV 139, which supports links identified by IPv6 addresses. RFC 6119 prohibits the use of TLV 139 when it is possible to use TLV 138.
sections.plainLanguage: The existing scheme has a fixed list of link attributes, each with a number, and a separate pair of advertisements for shared risk link groups. There is nothing in them to say which application is reading the values.

sections.title: The Application Identifier Bit Mask
sections.content:
Two codepoints are defined to support Application-Specific Link Attribute (ASLA) advertisements: an Application-Specific Link Attributes sub-TLV, and an Application-Specific SRLG TLV. To support them, an application identifier bit mask identifies the applications associated with a given advertisement. The identification uses two bit masks. One is for standard applications, where the meaning of each bit is defined in an IANA-controlled registry. A second is for non-standard User-Defined Applications (UDAs), which are not subject to standardization and are outside the scope of the document.

The encoding starts with a one-octet field holding the Standard Application Identifier Bit Mask length and a flag, then a one-octet field holding the User-Defined Application Identifier Bit Mask length and a flag, then the standard bit mask itself, which is between 0 and 8 octets, then the user-defined bit mask, also between 0 and 8 octets. The length of each mask SHOULD be the minimum required to send all bits that are set. The lengths are limited to 8 octets so that enough space is left to advertise the link attributes without overrunning the maximum length of a sub-TLV.

In the standard mask, bit 0 is the R-bit, set to specify RSVP-TE, bit 1 is the S-bit, set to specify SR Policy, and bit 2 is the F-bit, set to specify an LFA, which includes all LFA types. Undefined bits that are transmitted MUST be transmitted as 0 and MUST be ignored on receipt, bits that are not transmitted MUST be treated as if they were set to 0, and bits that an implementation does not support MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The new advertisements start with a small bit mask that names the applications in play. Each bit stands for one application: the first for RSVP-TE, the second for Segment Routing Policy, the third for loop-free alternates. The rest of the space is for applications that are not standardised.

sections.title: The Application-Specific Link Attributes Sub-TLV
sections.content:
A sub-TLV for TLVs Advertising Neighbor Information is defined with type 16, a variable one-octet length, and a value holding the application identifier bit mask followed by link attribute sub-sub-TLVs whose formats match those already defined in RFC 5305, RFC 7308 and RFC 8570. If the SABM Length or UDABM Length in the bit mask is greater than 8, the entire sub-TLV MUST be ignored.

When the mask length is non-zero and the L-flag is not set, all applications named in the mask MUST use the link attributes in the sub-TLV. When the L-flag is set, all applications named in the mask MUST use the legacy advertisements for the corresponding link, the link attribute sub-sub-TLVs for those applications MUST NOT be advertised, and any such sub-sub-TLVs MUST be ignored on receipt. The end result is that for a given application either the values in the new sub-sub-TLVs are used or the values in the legacy sub-TLVs are used, but not both.

Multiple sub-TLVs for the same link MAY be advertised and SHOULD advertise non-conflicting application and attribute pairs. A conflict exists when the same application is associated with two different values for the same link attribute for a given link. When conflicting values are advertised, the first advertisement received in the lowest-numbered Link State Protocol Data Unit MUST be used and subsequent advertisements of the same attribute MUST be ignored.

Link attributes MAY also be advertised with zero-length application identifier bit masks. Such advertisements MUST be used by standard applications and UDAs when no advertisement with a non-zero-length mask and a matching bit set is present for a given link, and MUST NOT be used otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: The sub-TLV holds the bit mask and then the attribute values themselves, in the same formats the old advertisements used. A flag in the mask says whether the applications named should read the new values or go back to the old advertisements, and a rule settles the case where two advertisements give the same application different values for the same attribute.

sections.title: The Application-Specific SRLG TLV
sections.content:
A TLV is defined to advertise application-specific SRLGs for a given link. Although similar in functionality to TLV 138 and TLV 139, this single TLV provides support for IPv4, IPv6 and unnumbered identifiers for a link. Unlike TLVs 138 and 139, it uses sub-TLVs to encode the link identifiers, so that the flexible formatting required for multiple identifier types can be supported.

The TLV has type 238, a one-octet length, and a value made up of the Neighbor System-ID and pseudonode ID in 7 octets, the application identifier bit mask, a one-octet length of the sub-TLVs, the Link Identifier sub-TLVs, and zero or more SRLG values of 4 octets each. If the mask lengths are greater than 8, the entire TLV MUST be ignored.

The Link Identifier sub-TLVs defined are type 4 link local and remote identifiers, type 6 IPv4 interface address, type 8 IPv4 neighbor address, type 12 IPv6 interface address and type 13 IPv6 neighbor address, with values chosen to match the equivalent sub-TLVs from RFC 5305, RFC 5307 and RFC 6119. At least one set of link identifiers MUST be present and multiple occurrences of the same identifier type MUST NOT be present, and TLVs that do not meet this requirement MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Shared risk link groups say which links fail together. The new advertisement carries those values for one link, identifies the link in a way that covers IPv4, IPv6 and unnumbered links, and carries the same application bit mask as the other new advertisement.

sections.title: Migrating from the Older Advertisements
sections.content:
All of the standard applications named by the new bit mask were deployed using the legacy advertisements before this document was written. They may continue to use the legacy advertisements for a given link so long as the application is RSVP-TE, or the application is SR Policy or LFA and RSVP-TE is not deployed anywhere in the network, or the application is SR Policy or LFA with RSVP-TE deployed and the sets of links and attribute values are fully congruent with those used by RSVP-TE. New applications defined by future documents MUST NOT make use of the legacy advertisements.

Routers that do not support the extensions process only legacy advertisements and are likely to infer that RSVP-TE is enabled on the links for which legacy advertisements exist. So long as there is any such router with any of the standard applications enabled, all routers MUST continue to advertise link attributes for those applications using only legacy advertisements, and application-specific advertisements for them MUST NOT be sent.

Once all the legacy routers have been upgraded, migration proceeds in three steps: send the new advertisements while continuing to advertise the legacy ones, so that receiving routers keep using the legacy advertisements; enable the use of the new advertisements on all routers; then remove the legacy advertisements. When the migration is complete it becomes possible to advertise incongruent values per application on a given link.
sections.plainLanguage: The new advertisements are optional and the old ones keep working, so a network can move over gradually. Until every router understands the new form, the old form must be used for the standard applications, and then the changeover is done in three steps: send both, switch to reading the new one, and finally stop sending the old one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security concerns for IS-IS are addressed in ISO 10589, RFC 5304 and RFC 5310. While IS-IS is deployed under a single administrative domain, there can be deployments where potential attackers have access to one or more networks in the IS-IS routing domain, and in those deployments the stronger authentication mechanisms defined in those documents SHOULD be used.

This document defines an improved way to advertise link attributes. Tampering with the information it defines may have an effect on the applications that use it, including impacting traffic engineering. Because the new advertisements limit the scope to specific applications, the impact of tampering is similarly limited in scope.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS is normally run inside one organisation, so it is trusted. Where that is not true, the stronger IS-IS authentication should be used. The new advertisements are narrower than the old ones, so a router that forges them can only mislead the applications named in the bit mask.
